claims.text: The paper proposes two training-free stochastic gates on SAE feature steering. STS draws an independent Bernoulli(p) gate at every position. SBS draws a single Bernoulli(p) gate per sequence that steers a leading window of size W all-or-nothing. Neither needs a reward model or a learned gating policy, and p interpolates between no steering and full steering.

Steering only a fraction of tokens with STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect. For LLaMA it recovers more than 95% of toxicity reduction at p=0.5 and more than 75% of emotion gains by p=0.7. The steering magnitude is calibrated once at p=1 and held fixed, so sparse results get no per-p re-tuning.

STS overtakes a deliberately strong, iteratively engineered prompting baseline in five of six model-task settings. The crossover ratio depends on the task. Sadness on Gemma-2 2B is the exception, where prompting stays ahead.

At matched nominal p, STS produces larger behavioral shifts than SBS. However, SBS realizes a much smaller fraction of steered tokens at the same p. Once realized budgets are matched, no single ordering holds: STS keeps an advantage on toxicity, while SBS is competitive on fear.

Fluency degradation (perplexity, Rep-3/Rep-4) grows monotonically with steering density, so sparse operating points cost less fluency than full steering. All methods are paired with fluency guards (norm preservation, clamping, repetition penalty), and an ablation shows these guards substantially cut perplexity and repetition.

The best-performing magnitude alpha* (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) rises as the intervention ratio falls. Residual-stream displacement grows with both p and alpha: p adds displaced positions, while alpha deepens displacement per token. This makes the two substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift.

The method differs from the concurrent SIA in several ways. It uses a fixed pretrained-SAE direction in the residual stream with no learned selector, auxiliary value model, or best-of-N. It produces a single completion with only a vector addition when the gate fires. Because protocols differ, SIA results are not directly comparable, and random gating serves as a control that selective methods should beat.

items.question: Take the realized ratio that the paper's matched-budget table reports for SBS with W=64 at p=0.5. Using SBS's gating rule, about what fraction of generated tokens are steered within a sequence whose gate actually fires? Why?
items.answer: About 0.52 (0.261 / 0.5). SBS draws a single gate per sequence, so about half the sequences receive no steering at all. The realized ratio therefore comes entirely from the steered half. Within those sequences, only the leading window of about 64 of the up-to-128 tokens is steered, which matches roughly half.
rubric: Gives roughly 0.5 (about 0.26 divided by 0.5)
Explains that SBS's single per-sequence gate leaves about half of sequences completely unsteered, so the realized ratio must be divided by p
Connects the result to steering being confined to the leading window (about 64 of 128 tokens)

history.question: Suppose the paper's SBS method is run on 100 prompts at p=0.5. Roughly how many of those sequences receive no steering at all? Explain why using SBS's gating rule.

answers.answer: About 50 sequences receive no steering. SBS draws one Bernoulli(p) gate per sequence, so at p=0.5 approximately half the sequences have their gate set to zero.

About 50 sequences. SBS draws a single Bernoulli(p) gate per sequence: with probability 1−p the whole sequence gets no steering at all, and only with probability p does it steer a contiguous window of W tokens. So at p=0.5 roughly half of the 100 sequences are entirely unsteered.

history.question: Take the realized ratio that the paper's matched-budget table reports for SBS with W=64 at p=0.5. Using SBS's gating rule, about what fraction of generated tokens are steered within a sequence whose gate actually fires? Why?

answers.answer: On a 128-token generation budget, SBS with W=64 and p=0.5 has a realized ratio of about \(0.5\cdot64/128=0.25\). Conditional on the gate firing, however, about 64 of 128 tokens—one half—are steered.

Within a sequence whose gate fires, essentially the entire W-token window is steered, so the steered fraction is ≈W/L (64 tokens of a maximum-length completion), not p. This is because SBS makes one Bernoulli(p) draw per block: p controls how often the gate fires, while W controls how many tokens each firing steers. I don't know the exact maximum length.

items.question: Take the realized ratio that the paper's matched-budget table reports for STS at p=0.3, together with the maximum generation length from the implementation details. About how many tokens of a maximum-length completion are actually steered? Why does the realized ratio differ slightly from p?
items.answer: About 37 tokens (0.287 × 128 ≈ 36.7). STS draws an independent Bernoulli(p) gate at each position, so p is only the expected fraction. The empirical fraction fluctuates randomly around p.
rubric: Gives roughly 36–37 tokens (0.287 × 128)
Explains that STS's independent per-token Bernoulli gates make p an expectation, so the realized fraction deviates randomly from 0.3

answers.answer: The implementation uses a maximum of 128 generated tokens. Thus STS at p=0.3 steers 0.3×128=38.4 tokens in expectation, or about 38–39 tokens.
With the implementation's maximum generation length of 128 tokens and STS's independent per-token Bernoulli(p) gating, the expected number of steered tokens at p=0.3 is 0.3×128 ≈ 38 tokens.

answers.answer: Assuming a realized ratio near 0.30 and a 128-token maximum, about 38 generated tokens are steered. The realized ratio can differ slightly from p because Bernoulli token sampling is finite-sample random and generated or eligible sequence lengths vary.

Roughly p×L tokens (about 0.3 of the completion) are steered, and the realized ratio deviates slightly from p because selection is stochastic over finite, variable-length generations—the realized figure is the fraction actually selected, not the nominal sampling probability.

items.question: A reader claims that SBS (W=32) and STS at p=0.9 should steer similar fractions of tokens because they share the same p. Using the paper's matched-budget table and SBS's definition, why is this wrong?
items.answer: The table shows realized ratios of about 0.27 for SBS W=32 and about 0.87 for STS at p=0.9. SBS draws one gate per sequence, and even when that gate fires it steers only the leading W positions, so its budget is bounded by the window. STS instead gates every position independently.
rubric: Cites the large gap in realized ratio (about 0.27 for SBS W=32 vs about 0.87 for STS)
Explains that SBS uses one all-or-nothing gate per sequence restricted to a leading window, whereas STS gates each position independently

history.question: A reader summarizes the paper's SBS as 'steering a random half of positions in each sequence when p=0.5.' Why is this summary wrong according to the paper's definition?

answers.answer: SBS applies p at the sequence level: with probability p it selects that sequence and then steers a contiguous W-token window; otherwise it steers none of that sequence. It does not independently select pW or a p-fraction of all positions in every sequence.

SBS's randomness is a sequence-level gate, not a per-position mask: at p=0.5 it steers one contiguous block of W tokens in about half the sequences and steers nothing in the other half. Randomly scattering half of the positions within every sequence describes STS's per-token Bernoulli gating, not SBS.

history.question: A reader claims that SBS (W=32) and STS at p=0.9 should steer similar fractions of tokens because they share the same p. Using the paper's matched-budget table and SBS's definition, why is this wrong?

answers.answer: The claim is wrong because STS applies p independently to each token, whereas SBS applies p to a block gate and steers W tokens when that gate fires. Thus SBS’s expected realized ratio is roughly \(pW/L\), much smaller than STS’s p for W=32.

The claim conflates gate probability with realized token fraction: in SBS, p is the probability that a block gate fires (steering one contiguous W-token window per sequence), not a per-token selection probability as in STS, so SBS's realized steered fraction is roughly p·W/L, far below p. The matched-budget table therefore shows SBS (W=32, p=0.9) steering a much smaller share of tokens than STS at p=0.9. I don't know the exact table values.

items.question: Use the paper's matched-budget table for Gemma-2 2B. Compute what fraction of STS's p=0.9 effect is already reached at p=0.5, once for toxicity and once for fear. What does the contrast say about how far the paper's redundancy finding extends?
items.answer: For toxicity the fraction is about 0.90 (0.237 / 0.263). For fear it is only about 0.43 (0.108 / 0.251). Redundancy is strong for toxicity suppression, but emotion elicitation needs a denser intervention. This matches the paper's statement that the required ratio is task-dependent and smaller for toxicity than for emotion.

Computes about 0.4 for fear

answers.answer: Approximately nine-tenths of STS's p=0.9 toxicity reduction is already present at p=0.5. This supports substantial redundancy for that setting, although the paper does not claim the same retention fraction for every task.

Roughly 90% — nearly all of STS's p=0.9 toxicity reduction is already achieved at p=0.5 (best guess at the exact figure). This is the paper's redundancy claim in miniature: half the interventions buy almost the full behavioral effect, so dense steering mostly just adds fluency cost.

On fear, STS at p=0.5 keeps a markedly smaller share of its p=0.9 effect (best guess: on the order of half to two-thirds), whereas on toxicity it keeps the large majority (~90% or more). history.question: Someone cites the paper's finding that STS at p=0.5 roughly doubles SBS (W=32) on fear as proof that token-level gating is intrinsically more efficient per steered token. Using the paper's matched-budget analysis, why is this inference unsupported?

answers.answer: That comparison is not budget-matched: with 128-token generations, SBS W=32 at p=0.5 steers only about 12.5% of tokens in expectation, versus 50% for STS. Once SBS W=64 at p=0.9 is compared at a similar realized ratio, the fear gap narrows sharply, so the raw doubling does not establish intrinsic token-level efficiency.

The raw-p comparison conflates budget with mechanism: SBS steers only W tokens within the fraction p of gated sequences, so at p=0.5, W=32 its realized ratio is roughly p·W/L (≈0.12 for ~128-token completions), far below STS's 0.5. In the paper's matched-budget table, where realized ratios are equated, the STS–SBS gap shrinks substantially (and nearly vanishes on toxicity), so the "intrinsic per-token efficiency" claim is unsupported — STS was mostly just steering more tokens.

items.question: The paper's fluency-preservation appendix names two ways the steered representation can drift off the natural activation manifold. Section 4.2 reports that the fluency-versus-ratio trend holds across SBS window sizes. Which of the two drift sources does this observation isolate? Which aspect of the paper's experimental protocol makes the comparison isolate that source?
items.answer: The appendix attributes drift either to growing steering strength or to the intervention accumulating across tokens. The magnitude alpha is calibrated once at p=1 and held fixed across all methods and ratios. Per-token strength is therefore constant, and the only thing that varies across STS and the SBS windows is how many positions are steered. Fluency tracking the realized ratio regardless of gating scheme thus reflects accumulation-driven drift, not a method-specific artifact.

history.question: The paper's implementation appendix describes how steered activations drift off the natural manifold. Using that description, why should steering fewer positions reduce fluency degradation?

answers.answer: Each intervention displaces a hidden state away from the distribution of naturally occurring activations, and repeated displacements can accumulate. Steering fewer positions reduces this cumulative drift and leaves unmodified tokens to anchor the continuation near the natural manifold.

Each steered position injects a fixed vector that pushes the residual stream off the natural activation manifold, and these deviations compound as later layers and positions build on perturbed states. Steering fewer positions creates fewer off-manifold points and lets the unsteered positions' ordinary dynamics pull the trajectory back toward the manifold, so cumulative drift — and hence perplexity degradation — is reduced.

history.question: The paper reports that its fluency-versus-ratio trend holds across SBS window sizes. Why does this fit the account of off-manifold drift given in its fluency-preservation appendix, rather than pointing to a method-specific artifact?

answers.answer: This supports the off-manifold-drift account because fluency tracks the realized fraction of steered tokens across different window sizes. If the same dose-response appears when the windowing pattern changes, cumulative activation displacement—not one selector’s implementation—is the likely cause.

If the fluency cost were a method-specific artifact it would vary with the windowing mechanism; instead the same fluency-versus-realized-ratio trend holds across SBS window sizes, so cost tracks how many tokens are displaced regardless of how they were chosen. That matches the appendix's account in which each steered token pushes the residual off its data manifold and cumulative drift scales with the number of displaced tokens.

history.question: The paper's fluency-preservation appendix names two ways the steered representation can drift off the natural activation manifold. Section 4.2 reports that the fluency-versus-ratio trend holds across SBS window sizes. Which of the two drift sources does this observation isolate? Which aspect of the paper's experimental protocol makes the comparison isolate that source?

answers.answer: I don't know the actual paper, but my best guess: the two drift sources are (i) steering too many positions (higher intervention ratio pushing activations off-manifold) and (ii) steering contiguous spans, which creates local discontinuities at block boundaries; the fact that the fluency-versus-ratio trend is invariant across SBS window sizes isolates the ratio (how many tokens are steered) as the operative source. The protocol feature that makes this work is varying window size while holding the realized intervention ratio fixed, so any contiguity/boundary effect would show up as a window-size dependence — and its absence pins the drift on density rather than arrangement.

This isolates cumulative intervention-ratio or “dose” drift rather than drift caused by a larger per-token steering displacement. Holding the steering vector, layer, and magnitude fixed while comparing SBS windows at matched realized ratios leaves the total fraction of edited representations—not the size of each edit—as the explanatory variable.

items.question: A reviewer argues that the paper's fluency advantage for sparse steering is really produced by its three fluency corrections. Where does full steering sit in the paper's fluency-versus-ratio results, and which conditions receive the corrections? Why does that combination rule out the reviewer's explanation?
items.answer: Full steering sits at the high end of both perplexity and repetition. Norm preservation, clamping and the repetition penalty are paired with every steering method and held fixed, including under full steering. Because full steering is also guarded yet remains the least fluent, the corrections cannot explain the trend across ratios. The differences come from steering density.
rubric: States that full steering has the highest perplexity and repetition
Notes that the corrections are applied identically to all methods and ratios, including full steering
Concludes that the fluency differences across ratios are due to density, not the guards

history.question: A reviewer suggests that the lower perplexity the paper finds at small intervention ratios is caused by its repetition penalty and other fluency guards, not by sparsity. Why does the paper's setup rule this out as an explanation of the trend across ratios?

answers.answer: The repetition penalty, decoding settings, and fluency guards are held fixed while p changes, so they cannot explain a systematic difference between ratios. The paper also reports the same qualitative trend in its fluency-preservation ablation.

The repetition penalty and other fluency guards are fixed decoding settings applied identically at every intervention ratio, including full steering at p=1. A factor held constant across conditions can shift the whole perplexity curve but cannot produce a monotone trend as p varies, so the perplexity improvement at small ratios must be attributed to sparsity itself.

Since full steering remains disfluent despite receiving the same corrections, the sparse-steering fluency advantage must come from steering fewer tokens, not from the corrections—ruling out the reviewer's explanation.

items.question: A reader argues: 'Because the paper's norm-preservation guard restores each steered activation to its original norm, a larger alpha cannot increase per-token displacement, so alpha* should not depend on p.' Using the paper's description of that guard and its residual-shift appendix, why is this argument wrong?
items.answer: Norm preservation only prevents magnitude inflation. The steered state is still rotated toward v, and a larger alpha rotates it further, so per-token displacement still grows with alpha, as the appendix's measurements show. Since p adds displaced positions while alpha deepens displacement per position, the two are substitutable. Lower p therefore calls for larger alpha, matching the rising alpha*.
rubric: Notes that norm preservation rotates the activation toward v rather than eliminating displacement, so larger alpha still deepens per-token displacement
Explains that p adds displaced positions while alpha deepens displacement per position, making them substitutable
Concludes that lower p requires larger alpha

history.question: A reader argues that lowering p should leave the ideal per-token magnitude unchanged, because p only controls how many tokens are steered. Using the paper's residual-stream shift analysis, why is this reasoning incomplete?

answers.answer: The residual analysis gives an expected cumulative shift proportional to pα along the injected direction, so reducing p reduces the mean shift as well as the number of interventions. Holding behavior fixed therefore generally requires a larger α, approximately compensating for lower p, subject to variance and nonlinear fluency effects.

The residual-stream analysis says behavior tracks the cumulative shift, which scales like α times the number of steered tokens (≈α·p·L) along the target direction. Lowering p shrinks the total shift even if per-token magnitude is unchanged, so the ideal α is not invariant to p — it must rise roughly as 1/p to produce the same shift.

history.question: A reader argues: 'Because the paper's norm-preservation guard restores each steered activation to its original norm, a larger alpha cannot increase per-token displacement, so alpha* should not depend on p.' Using the paper's description of that guard and its residual-shift appendix, why is this argument wrong?

answers.answer: Norm preservation fixes only the activation’s radius, not its direction or displacement. Increasing alpha can rotate the activation farther and increase the chord distance \(\|\tilde h-h\|\), so residual shift remains alpha-dependent and the optimal alpha can vary with p.

The guard rescales each steered activation back to its original norm but leaves the directional change intact, so increasing alpha still increases the angular/directional displacement per token even though the norm is clamped. The residual-shift analysis makes the expected shift proportional to p·alpha, so alpha* must depend on p; the reader wrongly assumes that norm preservation caps the displacement itself.

items.question: What alpha did the paper's calibration select for Gemma-2 2B fear steering, and where does that point lie on the calibration sweep's fluency curves? Use this to explain why the rising alpha* at low p does not license making alpha arbitrarily large.
items.answer: Alpha = 30, chosen just below the inflection where perplexity and Rep-3/Rep-4 spike sharply while the behavioral effect saturates. Alpha* is defined as maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation. Even if its optimum moves upward at lower p, alpha remains bounded by that fluency inflection.

Notes it sits just below a sharp inflection in perplexity and repetition, with behavioral gains saturating
Concludes that alpha* is fluency-constrained, so alpha cannot simply be increased without bound

history.question: Given how the paper defines alpha* in its magnitude-versus-ratio analysis, why does the rising trend at low p not imply that alpha should simply be made as large as possible?

answers.answer: α* is the empirically best magnitude at a given ratio, subject to behavioral saturation and fluency degradation, not an instruction to increase α without bound. Beyond α*, additional magnitude produces little behavioral gain and can push activations off-manifold or reduce task performance.

α* is defined as the fluency-constrained optimum — the magnitude giving the strongest behavioral effect before perplexity degrades unacceptably. Its rise at low p only means fewer steered tokens leave more fluency headroom to tolerate a larger α; pushing α past α* collapses fluency while behavior saturates or degrades, so "as large as possible" does not follow.

items.question: The residual-shift appendix's argument that p and alpha are substitutable depends on a property of the injected direction. Which step of the paper's steering-direction construction is supposed to provide that property, and what happens to substitutability if that step goes wrong?
items.answer: The property is that the injected direction is aligned with the target feature. It is supposed to come from the contrastive feature-selection step: ranking SAE features by mean activation differential between positive and neutral sets and aggregating the top-K decoder directions into a unit vector. If poor contrastive corpora or SAE quality yield non-discriminative features, added displacement from either alpha or p would not translate into the target behavior. Trading one for the other would then no longer be justified.
rubric: Identifies alignment of the direction with the target feature as the needed property
Attributes it to the contrastive top-K SAE feature selection (mean activation differential) and aggregation into v
Explains that misaligned or poorly chosen features would break the mapping from displacement to behavior, and thus break substitutability

history.question: The paper's residual-shift appendix argues that alpha and p are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift. Which premise of that argument would fail if the injected direction were not aligned with the target feature, and what would follow?

answers.answer: The argument assumes the injected vector has a nonzero projection onto the target behavioral feature. If it were orthogonal or misaligned, pα would produce no equivalent target-feature shift, and increasing either quantity would mainly amplify off-target perturbations.

The premise that fails is that the injected direction has a consistent positive projection onto the target feature direction, so each steered token adds the same signed increment and shifts accumulate linearly (∝α·p·L). Without that alignment, the increments do not add up toward the behavior — raising α or p would mostly inject off-target noise, buying fluency damage without behavioral gain, and the α↔p substitutability collapses.

history.question: The residual-shift appendix's argument that p and alpha are substitutable depends on a property of the injected direction. Which step of the paper's steering-direction construction is supposed to provide that property, and what happens to substitutability if that step goes wrong?

answers.answer: The appendix needs the injected direction to have a controlled fixed scale, and plausibly no uncontrolled radial component. The construction’s radial-component removal or orthogonalization, followed by unit normalization, is intended to provide that property; if it fails, norm preservation rescales different amounts of the injection as alpha changes, breaking clean p–alpha substitutability.

The required property is that the injected direction is unit-norm (and roughly orthogonal to typical residual directions) so per-token displacement scales linearly with alpha; the unit-normalization step of the direction construction is meant to provide this. If that step goes wrong, the norm-preservation guard rescales away part of the injected shift, effective displacement stops scaling linearly, and p–alpha substitutability breaks down. I don't know the paper's exact construction details.
